subject: paediatrics
title: Primitive Reflexes, Moro Response and Cranial Swellings

steps.tx: The most sensitive clinical indicator of neonatal neurological integrity is the **Moro reflex response**. Elicited by allowing the supported infant head to suddenly drop backward thirty degrees relative to the trunk, the response exhibits two distinct phases: initial rapid abduction and extension of the arms with hand opening, followed by smooth adduction and flexion accompanied by crying.
steps.say: The Moro reflex features arm extension and abduction followed by adduction and crying.

vis.alt: Clinical examination of six primitive neonatal reflexes.
vis.caption: Primitive neonatal reflexes including the Moro response and asymmetrical tonic neck reflex. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Unilateral failure of arm abduction defines an **asymmetrical Moro reflex**. This focal deficit points toward localized mechanical birth trauma, most frequently a fractured clavicle or brachial plexus traction injury like Erb palsy involving the fifth and sixth cervical roots. Complete bilateral absence of the Moro reflex indicates severe generalized central nervous system depression or asphyxia.
steps.say: An asymmetrical Moro reflex indicates birth trauma like clavicle fracture or Erb palsy.

rows: Waiter's tip hand, absent biceps jerk

steps.tx: After delivery, the umbilical stump is managed with **dry umbilical cord care**, keeping the base clean, dry, and exposed to room air without dressings. In high-mortality low-resource community settings, applying 7.1 percent chlorhexidine digluconate gel to the cord stump within twenty-four hours of birth substantially reduces the incidence of omphalitis and all-cause neonatal mortality.
steps.say: Dry cord care is standard, with chlorhexidine gel recommended in high-mortality community settings.

left.title: Standard Institutional Care
points: Keep cord stump clean and dry
Expose base to air, fold nappy below stump

right.title: Chlorhexidine in High-Risk Settings
points: Applied daily for the first week of life
Prevents fatal bacterial omphalitis and sepsis

steps.tx: Severe ascending bacterial colonization of the umbilical stump produces **neonatal omphalitis**, characterized by periumbilical erythema, edema, tenderness, and foul-smelling purulent discharge. Pathogens include Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and enteric Gram-negative bacilli. Untreated omphalitis rapidly spreads along the patent umbilical vein, causing portal vein thrombosis, peritonitis, and overwhelming systemic septic shock.
steps.say: Omphalitis presents with periumbilical erythema and can progress rapidly to portal vein thrombosis and sepsis.

rows: Purulent umbilical discharge, no skin flare
Emergency surgical debridement and broad-spectrum IV

steps.tx: A common benign swelling resulting from mechanical vaginal compression is **caput succedaneum formation**. Representing diffuse serosanguinous subcutaneous edema superficial to the epicranial aponeurosis, it is present immediately at birth, pits on digital palpation, and freely crosses cranial suture lines. Caput succedaneum requires no treatment and resolves spontaneously within forty-eight to seventy-two hours.
steps.say: Caput succedaneum is soft subcutaneous edema that crosses suture lines and resolves in three days.

vis.alt: Anatomical cross section comparing caput succedaneum, cephalhematoma, and subgaleal haemorrhage.
vis.caption: Anatomical layers of neonatal scalp swellings distinguishing caput from cephalhematoma. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Subperiosteal hemorrhage over a cranial bone produces a **neonatal cephalhematoma**, arising from the rupture of subperiosteal capillary vessels during instrumented or prolonged labor. Characteristically, the swelling is strictly limited by the periosteal attachments at cranial suture lines, typically overlying a parietal bone. It appears hours after birth and resolves slowly over several weeks.
steps.say: Cephalhematoma is a subperiosteal bleed restricted by cranial suture lines that takes weeks to resolve.

rows: Present at the moment of birth
Develops gradually hours to days post-delivery
Strictly confined by cranial suture boundaries
Resolves over 2 to 8 weeks, may calcify

steps.tx: As red blood cells trapped within a large cephalhematoma undergo enzymatic breakdown, the infant faces **increased hyperbilirubinemia risk**. Heme oxygenase degrades hemoglobin into unconjugated bilirubin, overwhelming immature neonatal hepatic glucuronidation. Clinicians must closely monitor transcutaneous and serum bilirubin levels, as severe cephalhematomas frequently necessitate early phototherapy.
steps.say: Breakdown of RBCs within a cephalhematoma releases bilirubin, raising phototherapy requirements.

right.title: Clinical Surveillance
points: Avoid needle aspiration due to infection risk

steps.tx: The most dangerous extracranial neonatal collection is **subgaleal haemorrhage**, where blood accumulates within the loose areolar tissue between the galea aponeurotica and periosteum. Bleeding crosses suture lines, extending from the orbital ridges to the nape of the neck. Because this potential space can accommodate the infant's entire circulating blood volume, it precipitates rapidly fatal hypovolemic shock.
steps.say: Subgaleal hemorrhage spreads across the entire cranium and can cause fatal hypovolemic shock.

rows: Massive, spreads from orbits to neck
Diffuse, fluctuant fluid wave on palpation
Immediate aggressive blood transfusion and ICU triage
